name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
title: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
answer: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the practice of running heavy analytical workloads, such as model training, simulation, and statistical estimation, against datasets that an organisation holds under its own control rather than against public or scraped sources. The data is typically licensed, proprietary, or sensitive, which means the compute cannot simply be rented from a public cloud without contractual and technical safeguards. The scope spans the pipeline from data access and storage through scheduling and execution to the capture of results and their provenance. It sits at the meeting point of quantitative analysis, research reproducibility, and research computing infrastructure.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the practice of running heavy analytical workloads, such as model training, simulation, and statistical estimation, against datasets that an organisation holds under its own control rather than against public or scraped sources. The data is typically licensed, proprietary, or sensitive, which means the compute cannot simply be rented from a public cloud without contractual and technical safeguards. The scope spans the pipeline from data access and storage through scheduling and execution to the capture of results and their provenance. It sits at the meeting point of quantitative analysis, research reproducibility, and research computing infrastructure.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on clusters of CPUs and GPUs, often managed by a scheduler such as Slurm, with shared storage for datasets and scratch space for intermediate results. Institutional data usually stays inside a controlled network boundary, so compute is placed in an on-premises data centre, a private cloud, or a governed enclave rather than a general-purpose public service. Container images and environment files pin the software stack so that a run can be repeated months later. Access is mediated by identity and role, and jobs are queued rather than run interactively when the workload is large.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners begin by profiling the data and the computation to decide what must be parallelised and what can be batched. They write jobs as scripts or workflow definitions, submit them to the scheduler, and track runs through logs, metrics, and versioned configuration. Intermediate artefacts are written to durable storage so that a failed run can resume rather than restart. Results are tied back to the exact code commit, data snapshot, and parameter set that produced them, which is what makes the analysis reproducible. Review and handover depend on those records being readable by someone who did not run the job.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Institutional data carries obligations that follow it into every compute environment, including consent terms, data protection rules, and contractual limits on where processing may occur. Provenance records must show which dataset version was used, who authorised access, and what transformations were applied. Outputs derived from sensitive inputs may themselves be restricted, so release decisions are made deliberately rather than by default. Audit trails, retention schedules, and access reviews are part of normal operation, and the site links to original papers rather than to a search tool when citing the underlying research.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward finer-grained control over where computation happens, with confidential computing, federated approaches, and policy-aware schedulers allowing analysis to move closer to the data instead of the reverse. Reproducibility tooling is becoming more standard, so that a published result can be re-executed against the same governed inputs under the same conditions. Energy use and cost per run are increasingly reported alongside accuracy, because large workloads are judged on more than their output. Institutions are also building shared internal platforms so that teams do not each rebuild the same access, storage, and scheduling layers.
